equivalent_reason: Path.walk forwards on_error directly to os.walk (verified via inspect.getsource on Python 3.14). os.walk's documented and implemented behavior is: "By default errors from the os.scandir() call are ignored" when onerror is None, and if onerror is provided it is called with the OSError but the walk continues regardless (no return value is used to alter behavior). Both `on_error=None` and `on_error=lambda _: None` result in the OSError being swallowed and the walk continuing identically — there is no code path where these two produce different dirs/files/roots. Hence no test (unit or otherwise) can observe a difference, making this mutant equivalent.

Path.walk() delegates to os.walk(), passing on_error through as the onerror callback. Both CPython's os.walk and pathlib.Path.walk only invoke this callback for its side effects (e.g. logging or re-raising) when an OSError occurs while scanning a directory; the callback's return value is never read or used to alter control flow. Since neither lambda raises or has any other side effect, and both return values (None vs 0) are discarded identically, there is no observable difference in behavior between the original and mutated code under any input, including error conditions. No test can distinguish them.

Python's text codec lookup (used internally by str.encode/decode and Path.read_text) normalizes encoding names by lowercasing and collapsing separators before resolving the codec (see encodings.normalize_encoding / codecs.lookup). "utf-8" and "UTF-8" therefore resolve to the identical codec and produce byte-for-byte identical decoded output for any file content. No observable behavior differs, so no test — however constructed — can distinguish the original from the mutant. Verified empirically: decoding the same bytes with encoding="utf-8" vs encoding="UTF-8" gives identical results.

The `flow` argument to PyYAML's `Emitter.increase_indent` only changes behavior in the branch `if self.indent is None: self.indent = self.best_indent if flow else 0` — i.e. it only matters for the very first `increase_indent` call of the whole emission, before `self.indent` is set for the first time. For every subsequent call the `elif not indentless` branch is taken and `flow` is irrelevant. `render_yaml` always calls `yaml.dump(merged_dict, ...)` with `merged_dict: dict[str, Any]` as the document root. For any non-empty root dict, the very first `increase_indent` call comes from `expect_block_mapping`, which calls `self.increase_indent(flow=False)` explicitly (hardcoded in PyYAML's emitter, unrelated to the override) — so the override's `flow` parameter is already `False` on both the original and mutated code paths, producing identical output. For the one edge case where the root dict is empty (`{}`), PyYAML instead takes the flow-mapping path (`increase_indent(flow=True)`) while `self.indent is None`, which is where original and mutant diverge internally (`best_indent` vs `0`) — but since the mapping is empty, no indented content is ever written for that node, so the divergence in the internal `self.indent` value never surfaces in the emitted text (verified empirically: `render_yaml({})` produces `'--- {}\n'` under both the original and the hand-rolled mutant implementation, and a more complex document containing nested `[]`/`{}` values plus nested lists produced byte-identical output under both implementations). Since `render_yaml` is the sole caller/consumer of this Dumper and always passes a dict, there is no reachable input for which the mutation changes observable output; it is behaviorally equivalent.

`_PrecommitDumper` registers `_semantic_dict_representer` as the representer for `dict`, and that function always builds its own explicitly ordered `list[(k, v), ...]` and passes it to `dumper.represent_mapping(...)`. PyYAML's `represent_mapping` only applies its internal `sort_keys` sorting when the passed mapping has an `.items()` attribute (`if hasattr(mapping, "items"): if self.sort_keys: mapping = sorted(mapping.items())`); since a plain list of tuples has no `.items()`, that branch never executes, so `self.sort_keys` is never consulted for any mapping produced through this custom representer — including the top-level dict and every nested dict (repo entries, hook entries), all of which are plain `dict` and thus routed through the same representer. I verified empirically that `yaml.dump(d, Dumper=_PrecommitDumper, ..., sort_keys=False, ...)` and the same call without `sort_keys` produce byte-identical output for a dict containing out-of-order/unsorted keys at both top level and nested hook level. Therefore `sort_keys=False` is dead configuration in this code path and no test (however crafted) can distinguish its presence from its absence — the mutant is behaviorally equivalent.

`render_yaml` registers a custom representer (`_semantic_dict_representer`) for the `dict` type on `_PrecommitDumper`. This representer always computes its own explicit key ordering (priority-key list plus alphabetically-sorted remainder) and calls `dumper.represent_mapping(tag, [(k, data[k]) for k in ordered])`, passing a plain `list` of tuples rather than a dict. PyYAML's `BaseRepresenter.represent_mapping` only applies its internal `sort_keys`-driven sort when the passed `mapping` argument has an `.items()` method (i.e., is still a dict-like object); since a list of tuples has no `.items()`, that internal sort step is always skipped regardless of the `sort_keys` flag passed to `yaml.dump`. Every dict value in `merged_dict` (including nested ones) is a plain `dict`, so every mapping node in the document is produced via this custom representer. I verified empirically that `yaml.dump(d, Dumper=_PrecommitDumper, sort_keys=False, ...)` and the same call with `sort_keys=True` produce byte-identical output for representative nested dict structures (including keys not in the priority lists). Since `render_yaml`'s only callers (`gpc_init/generator.py` and the test suite) always pass plain `dict` instances, no input can make `sort_keys` observably affect the output, so the mutant is behaviorally equivalent to the original.
